nameStory: Cornflower earned its name from its habit of growing wild in European grain fields - 'corn' being the old-world term for cereal grains like wheat and barley. Its other popular name, bachelor's button, comes from the Victorian tradition where young men would wear these bright blue flowers in their lapels to show they were single and available for courtship!
description: Cornflower is a cheerful annual wildflower famous for its brilliant electric-blue blooms that seem to glow in sunlight. This slender, upright plant grows 1-3 feet tall with narrow, grayish-green leaves and distinctive spiky flower heads. Originally from Europe, it has naturalized across New England and blooms from late spring through fall, creating patches of intense blue color in fields and roadsides.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Brilliant electric-blue flower heads with deeply fringed, irregular petals that feel papery to the touch, sitting atop spiky green bracts that look like tiny pinecones

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves with a soft, woolly texture and grayish-green color that feels slightly fuzzy when rubbed between your fingers

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Slender, upright stems that branch near the top, creating an open, airy appearance with flowers held well above the foliage

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Flower heads measure about 1-2 inches across and have a subtle, sweet honey-like fragrance that's most noticeable on warm, still days

habitat: Look for cornflower in disturbed soils like old fields, roadsides, and garden edges where it has room to self-seed. It thrives in sunny, well-drained spots and poor to average soils, often appearing alongside other European wildflowers like chicory and Queen Anne's lace. You'll rarely find it in deep woods or wetlands.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes of fuzzy, grayish leaves. First blooms typically appear in late spring, with the distinctive blue flowers opening on warm, sunny days.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with masses of electric-blue flowers that attract bees and butterflies. Plants continue producing new flowers throughout the summer heat.
seasonality.fall: Flowers persist into early fall, gradually forming small, bristly seed heads. Seeds ripen to a silvery-brown color and disperse on autumn winds.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back completely, leaving only seeds in the soil to germinate the following spring.

funFact: Cornflower petals are completely edible and have a mild, sweet flavor - they're often used to add a stunning blue color to salads, teas, and even wedding cakes, making them one of the few truly blue foods in nature!
confusionNotes: Wild chicory also has bright blue flowers, but chicory blooms are flat and daisy-like, while cornflower heads are spiky and thistle-like. Remember: cornflower feels fuzzy, chicory feels smooth, and chicory flowers close up by afternoon while cornflowers stay open all day.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse the grain 'corn' in cornflower's name with American corn (maize) - in Europe, 'corn' means any cereal grain like wheat or oats. This flower was actually considered a serious agricultural weed before modern farming practices nearly drove it extinct in its native Europe.
compareHints: Unlike its knapweed cousins that have pink, purple, or yellow flowers, cornflower is the only member of this genus with true electric-blue blooms. Other knapweeds also tend to have more aggressive, weedy growth habits, while cornflower is gentler and more garden-friendly. The spiky bracts under the flower head are similar across all knapweeds, but cornflower's are typically greener and less papery than spotted or brown knapweed.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's knapweeds, spotted knapweed is distinguished by those characteristic dark spots or stripes on its flower bracts, while black knapweed has completely dark bracts and cornflower has much larger, showier blue flowers.

Among its knapweed relatives, brown knapweed stands out with its consistently star-shaped flowers, while black knapweed looks more brush-like and spotted knapweed has more deeply divided leaves with distinctive black-spotted bracts.
Among its knapweed relatives in New England, perennial cornflower stands out with its bright blue-purple color and usually entire leaves.
Black knapweed is distinguished from spotted knapweed by its solid-colored leaves (spotted knapweed has deeply lobed, almost ferny leaves) and its darker, more fringed flower bracts.
Among New England's knapweeds, Tyrol knapweed is distinguished by its very short-fringed, dark-edged bracts around the flower base.
Giant knapweed stands out dramatically from other New England knapweeds by its massive size and bright yellow color - most other knapweeds have purple, blue, or pink flowers that are much smaller.
